name: Zhurong
short_status: Silent since 18 May 2022, when it hibernated for the Martian winter after 358 sols and 1,921 m against a design life of 90. Dust is the likely cause, and as of 24 September 2026 China has declared no formal end.
tagline: CNSA (China) · China · Rover · 2021 · Multipolar Mars Ended
stats: sols worked, against a design life of 90
on the odometer when it went into hibernation

facts.label: Landing
facts.value: 14 May 2021 at 23:18 UT, which is 15 May at 07:18 Beijing time. The entry capsule separated from the Tianwen-1 orbiter and ran about nine minutes of autonomous entry, descent and landing.

facts.label: Landing site
facts.value: 109.925 E, 25.066 N, elevation -4,099.4 m, in southern Utopia Planitia near the highland-lowland boundary and a set of suspected ancient shorelines. The fix was determined after landing from sub-metre images taken by the orbiter's High Resolution Imaging Camera.

facts.label: Where they were aiming
facts.value: The pre-landing target was the centre of a landing ellipse to the north; the rover came down about 3.1 km south of the centre of ellipse 16, per English Wikipedia's account of the mission.

facts.label: Rover
facts.value: About 240 kg, six wheels, fold-out solar panels, a dish antenna on a rear mast and navigation, terrain and multispectral cameras on a front mast. Chinese Wikipedia gives the deployed dimensions as 2.6 m long, 3 m wide and 1.85 m high.

facts.label: Instruments
facts.value: Six: the Navigation and Terrain Camera (NaTeCam), the Multispectral Camera (MSCam), the Mars Surface Composition Detector (MarSCoDe, a laser-induced breakdown spectrometer with a shortwave infrared spectrometer), the Rover Subsurface Penetrating Radar (RoPeR), the Mars Rover Magnetometer (RoMAG) and the Mars Climate Station (MCS).

facts.label: Drive-off
facts.value: 22 May 2021 at 02:40 UT (10:40 Beijing). It imaged the landing platform, took a group portrait with it using a deployed camera, and started south.

facts.label: Design mission complete
facts.value: By 15 August 2021 Zhurong had worked 90 sols, about 92 Earth days, and driven 889 m, completing its planned survey with all payloads operating. Everything after that was extended mission.

facts.label: Solar conjunction
facts.value: Both the rover and the orbiter went quiet from late September to late October 2021 while Mars passed behind the Sun as seen from Earth, an expected and planned outage. CNSA confirmed on 22 October 2021 that both had come through it safely.

facts.label: Total distance
facts.value: 1,921 m on the onboard odometer. Xinhua, carrying People's Daily, reported the figure on 16 May 2022 at 356 sols; Zhang Rongqiao gave the same 1,921 m against 358 sols after hibernation. A March 2025 outreach article from the Chinese Academy of Sciences planetary mapping laboratory reported a visually reconstructed traverse: the rover travelled 2,009 m in total, 88 m more than the 1,921 m recorded by the onboard odometer, the discrepancy caused by wheel slippage due to the downslope trend of the traverse, in a study published in the IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing. So 1,921 m is the odometer figure of record and 2,009 m the image-based reconstruction of the same drive; the two measure different things.

facts.label: Data returned
facts.value: About 940 GB of raw science data across the whole Tianwen-1 mission as of 15 May 2022, per Xinhua. A later Xinhua report of 18 September 2022 gives 1,480 GB. The two figures are four months apart and cover the orbiter as well as the rover.

facts.label: Hibernation
facts.value: 18 May 2022, entered autonomously as the Utopia Planitia winter closed in. English Wikipedia dates it 20 May 2022; Zhang Rongqiao, chief designer of China's planetary exploration programme, said 18 May in an interview broadcast on 25 April 2023, and we follow him.

facts.label: Winter conditions
facts.value: Xinhua reported in May 2022 that daytime highs in the rover's area had fallen below -20 C, nights to -100 C, and dust events had become frequent, with solar input falling and heating demand rising.

facts.label: Wake-up conditions
facts.value: Zhang Rongqiao gave two thresholds that both had to be met for autonomous wake-up: internal temperature above -15 C, and solar generation reaching 140 W, the rover's minimum daily need. When both were satisfied the rover would switch itself on.

facts.label: Why it did not wake
facts.value: Zhang Rongqiao said in April 2023 that the most likely cause was unforeseen dust accumulation reducing power generation below the wake-up threshold. He described the design margins in the same interview: dust beyond about 20 per cent of the design allowance and generation is insufficient, beyond about 30 per cent and it would only work at peak sunlight, and beyond about 40 per cent the rover would never wake. He added that the outcome was within what the team had expected.

facts.label: Water on the surface
facts.value: Liu Yang's team at the National Space Science Center used MarSCoDe shortwave infrared spectra and camera data to identify rock-like plated duricrust rich in hydrated sulphates at the landing site, published in Science Advances in May 2022. Xinhua described it as the first in-situ detection of hydrated minerals on Mars by a rover-mounted shortwave infrared spectrometer.

facts.label: Ice beneath the site, 2026
facts.value: On 3 March 2026 CNSA announced that Zhurong's subsurface radar had found a low-loss layer about 7 m thick at roughly 15 m depth, interpreted as dirty ice, published in Earth and Planetary Science Letters as Evidence of shallow subsurface ice at Tianwen-1 landing site. Data returned in 2021 and 2022 is still producing results.

timeline: 23:18 UT: the entry capsule lands in southern Utopia Planitia after roughly nine minutes of autonomous descent. China becomes the third country to land a working spacecraft on Mars, after the Soviet Union and the United States.
With the ramp, mast, solar panels and directional antenna already deployed on landing day, the rover senses its surroundings and runs mobility self-checks.
02:40 UT: Zhurong rolls onto the surface and begins its survey, heading south towards the suspected ancient shoreline.
90 sols complete, 889 m driven, all payloads operating. The design mission is over and the extended mission begins.
Solar conjunction. Rover and orbiter both sit in safe mode while Mars is behind the Sun, then resume.

One Earth year on the surface: 356 sols worked, 1,921 m driven, about 940 GB of raw science data returned by the mission as a whole. Winter is closing in and the rover is preparing to switch to winter mode.
Zhurong hibernates autonomously at 358 sols. It is expected to wake itself around December 2022 once temperature and power both recover.
The projected wake-up window passes with no signal.

Zhang Rongqiao tells CCTV the rover is still asleep, gives the two wake-up conditions, and names unforeseen dust accumulation as the most likely reason it has not met them. This is the closest thing to an official end-of-mission statement.

The planetary mapping laboratory of the Chinese Academy of Sciences Aerospace Information Research Institute publishes the Zhurong visual-localisation result in an outreach article: a reconstructed traverse of 2,009 m against the odometer's 1,921 m, the 88 m difference caused by wheel slippage due to the downslope trend of the traverse. The study is published in the IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing.

CNSA announces that Zhurong's subsurface radar found a roughly 7 m low-loss layer at about 15 m depth in the landing area, interpreted as dirty ice and published in Earth and Planetary Science Letters.

Five years since the landing. The rover remains silent, and CNSA's news index, checked on 24 September 2026, carries no statement on Zhurong's status and no formal declaration that the mission is over.

images.caption: A crop of the deployable-camera portrait showing the Zhurong rover alone: the butterfly-wing solar arrays, the mast with the navigation and terrain cameras, the directional antenna and the six wheels.

images.caption: A colour panorama of southern Utopia Planitia from Zhurong, showing bright wind-shaped sand ridges running across a rock-strewn plain to a flat horizon, with part of the rover's own hardware in the lower left of the frame.
images.credit: He Zhu, National Science Review, CC BY 4.0; imagery CNSA / China Lunar Exploration Program (Zhurong)

images.caption: A wide-angle hazard-avoidance camera view from Zhurong showing two lines of wheel tracks running back across the plain, with a red box drawn at upper left around the discarded backshell and parachute of the entry capsule.
images.credit: CNSA / China Lunar Exploration Program (Zhurong hazard-avoidance camera). No individual photographer; the frame is camera-generated.

images.caption: HiRISE image of southern Utopia Planitia acquired on 11 March 2022 in which the Zhurong rover's entire southward traverse of roughly 1.5 km can be traced as a pair of wheel tracks on the surface.

PIA24914, a HiRISE view of Utopia Planitia acquired on 1 August 2021 and projected at 25 centimetres per pixel, showing the flat plain south of the landing site with impact craters, light-toned wind-blown ridges and troughs.
A HiRISE cutout from 6 June 2021 showing the discarded heat shield of the Tianwen-1 entry capsule lying on the surface of southern Utopia Planitia, with the dark impact mark it made on landing.
